segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus had finished giving instructions to his twelve disciples, he moved on from there to teach and proclaim in their towns.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now when John heard in prison about the deeds of the Messiah, he sent word through his disciples

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and asked him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Are you the one who is coming, or are we to expect someone else?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go and report to John what you hear and see:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: the blind see again and the lame walk, lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, the dead are raised and the poor have good news announced to them.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And blessed is anyone who does not stumble because of me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As they were going away, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “What did you go out into the wilderness to look at? A reed shaken by the wind?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Then what did you go out to see? Someone dressed in soft clothes? Look, those who wear soft clothes are in the houses of kings.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Then why did you go out? To see a prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: This is the one about whom it is written: ‘Look, I am sending my messenger before your face, who will prepare your way ahead of you.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Truly I tell you, among those born of women no one greater than John the Baptist has arisen; yet the least in the kingdom of the heavens is greater than he is.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: From the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of the heavens has been suffering violence, and the violent are seizing it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and if you are willing to accept it, he is Elijah, who is to come.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Let anyone who has ears hear.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But to what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplaces who call out to the others

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and say, ‘We played the pipe for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not mourn.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Look, a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ Yet wisdom is vindicated by her deeds.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he began to reproach the towns in which most of his miracles had taken place, because they had not turned back.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the miracles that took place in you had taken place in Tyre and Sidon, they would have turned back long ago in sackcloth and ashes.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But I tell you, it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? No, you will go down to Hades. For if the miracles that took place in you had taken place in Sodom, it would have remained to this day.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But I tell you that it will be more bearable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment than for you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At that time Jesus said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I praise you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and intelligent and revealed them to little children.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Yes, Father, for this is what was pleasing in your sight.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Everything has been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Come to me, all you who toil and are burdened, and I will give you rest.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For my yoke is easy to bear, and my burden is light.”

notes.note: Here the word has the article and works as a title for the anointed king Israel was expecting; John's question in the next verse is whether Jesus is that figure. 'Messiah' conveys the title to a modern reader, where 'Christ' tends to be heard as a name. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels.

Jesus answers by listing what is happening, in language drawn from Isaiah's pictures of God's coming restoration (Isaiah 35:5–6; 61:1; compare 26:19). A hearer who knew those passages would take the list as an indirect yes to John's question.

The Greek word covers a range of skin conditions, not only the disease now called leprosy. Under the law of Moses such conditions made a person ritually unclean and cut them off from ordinary community life, which is why the text speaks of being 'cleansed' and not simply healed.

notes.traditional: is not offended in me; takes no offense at me
notes.note: The verb means to trip someone up or bring about their fall, and in the Gospels it usually refers to being turned away from trust or loyalty. 'Offended' now suggests hurt feelings, which is too weak. Some modern translations also use 'stumble' or 'fall away' here.

notes.phrase: I am sending my messenger before your face
notes.note: The quotation follows Malachi 3:1, with wording that also echoes Exodus 23:20. The same book closes with a promise that God would send the prophet Elijah before the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5), which lies behind verse 14. 'Before your face' is a Hebrew idiom for 'ahead of you'.

The Greek is plural, reflecting a Hebrew and Aramaic way of speaking that a first-century hearer would have noticed. Most translations flatten it to 'heaven'. The plural is kept here wherever Matthew uses it for God's dwelling.

notes.traditional: suffers violence, and the violent take it by force
notes.note: This is one of the most disputed sentences in the Gospels. The verb can be passive ('suffers violence', that is, is attacked by opponents) or middle ('forces its way forward'), and those who 'seize' the kingdom may be enemies plundering it or eager people pressing into it. The rendering takes both clauses in the hostile sense, which fits the usually negative tone of the Greek words for 'violent people' and 'seize' and John's imprisonment in the context. The positive reading has serious scholarly support.

Greek has one word-family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice, justify). Here the verb means to be shown to be in the right, which 'vindicated' says more clearly than 'justified'. Many modern translations have 'vindicated' or 'proved right'.

Many manuscripts read 'by her children', matching the parallel saying in Luke 7:35. The earliest witnesses to Matthew read 'deeds', and most editors think 'children' was introduced by copyists to bring Matthew into line with Luke. 'Deeds' picks up 'the deeds of the Messiah' in verse 2.

'Repent' now centres on feeling sorry. In the Gospels the word carries the prophets' call to return to God, a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep 'repent' as an established term that readers understand to include a change of life.
'Meek' now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes someone who is gentle and not self-assertive. 'Gentle' or 'humble' is the usual rendering in modern translations.

A yoke is the wooden frame that harnesses working animals to a load. In Jewish wisdom writing it was a familiar image for accepting instruction (Sirach 51:26 invites the reader to put their neck under wisdom's yoke), and later Jewish teachers spoke of the yoke of the Law. 'You will find rest for your souls' echoes Jeremiah 6:16.

candidates.reason: Recurs across the Gospels and Paul, and translations vary between 'offend', 'cause to stumble', 'fall away' and 'cause to sin', which hides that one image is in play.
In the plural for Jesus' acts, translations vary between 'miracles', 'mighty works' and 'deeds of power', and the choice should be kept distinct from the renderings of σημεῖον and ἔργον.
The word covers skin conditions wider than modern leprosy, so the choice between 'leper' and a broader phrase needs to be made once for the Gospels.
It ranges over 'life', 'self' and 'soul', and 'soul' can import a later body-soul dualism, so the default and its alternates need fixing across the New Testament.
Jesus' main self-designation recurs in all four Gospels, and whether to keep the traditional title or render it differently should be decided once.
